2 1. Old quantum physics

 Appendix 1.E Exercises 52

 In this first chapter, some experiments and theoretical models that
started to form the first ideas and notions of the quantum and subatomic
world will be presented. This set of ideas is currently known as old quan-
tum physics and began at the very end of the 19th century (with the first
observations of spectral lines of Hydrogen gas) until the early decades of
the 20th century (with the de Broglie hypothesis, which proposed the wave
nature of matter). The old quantum physics represents the first cycle and
birth of quantum physics, being described in this chapter. Thereafter, the
quantum theory was formalized with the proposal and development of
Schrödinger’s equation, which will be addressed in the next chapter. Nat-
urally, many physical consequences emerged from this new theory, a topic
to be addressed along this book.
 Objective The goal of this chapter is to offer for the students a com-
 prehensive introduction to the historical principles of the old quantum
 physics. The concepts covered include the experimental basis, the Bohr
 model for the atom, and the semi-classical quantization rules. In Ap-
 pendix 1.C, a timeline with a historical retrospective of the scientific
 events discussed throughout the chapter is presented; while in Ap-
 pendix 1.D, a detailed summary is presented.

 1.1 Experimental basis

 Along this section, several experiments that provided evidence of the
quantum world will be explored and explained, connecting them with
the respective theoretical explanations existing at that time. As mentioned,
these experiments provided enough evidence for the construction of new
hypotheses and models that culminated, in the mid-twenties of the 20th
century, with the beginning of Modern Quantum Theory.

1.1.1 Double slit with light
 In 1801, Thomas Young observed that, when shining light through slits,
a typical pattern of wave interference occurs. More precisely, when using
two slits, the waves produce a constructive and destructive interference
pattern, expected for wave mechanics, and not for corpuscular mechanics.
Such experiment reinforced the ideas that light would be a wave. Later,
in 1865, James Maxwell demonstrated that, using a set of equations,1 light
1 Which are today jointly named after him.

1.1.2 Spectral lines of Hydrogen atom

tion of light through a prism, as shown in Fig. 1.1(a). As a result of this
decomposition, it was observed that a continuous spectrum derived from
white light was composed of all wavelengths.
 Two hundred years after Newton’s studies, the Swiss mathematician
Johann Balmer observed that, when an electrical discharge is applied to a
Hydrogen gas ampoule, a discrete color pattern is obtained, in opposition
to the continuous spectrum of the white light source. See Fig. 1.1(b). In
1885, based on these observations, Balmer developed a formula, which is
named after him, to describe the spectral lines of Hydrogen atom. This
empirical equation derives from the observation that the wavelength of
a certain line could be estimated through a relation with integers. More
precisely, Balmer proposed the following:

and m > 2 an integer. Balmer’s observations refer to lines with n = 2 (con-
stant) and m variable, however, an integer. See Table 1.1(a). There are other
emissions in the Balmer series, in addition to those described in the afore-
mentioned table. Nonetheless, they are in the ultraviolet band, outside the
visible band (m ≥ 7).
 Few years later, in 1888, Johannes Rydberg developed a formula (named
after him) to generalize the Balmer series and considering all series ob-

 ! The historical importance of these works lies in the empirical de-
 velopment of equations that relate the wavelength of the observed
 line to integers and, more importantly, these observations are re-
 lated to the electronic orbits in the atom.

 ! Johann Balmer (1825–1898): Born in Lausen, Switzerland. He was a
 mathematician and his main contribution to science was the studies
 on spectral lines of Hydrogen by developing, in 1885, the Balmer
 Formula.
 Johannes Rydberg (1854–1919): Born in Halmstad, Sweden. His
 contribution to science was the generalization, in 1888, of Balmer’s
 works, by developing a single equation for all spectral series of Hy-
 drogen.

1.1.3 Electron charge-to-mass ratio
 In 1897, Joseph Thomson, while studying cathode rays, confirmed, af-
ter William Crookes’s and other scientists’ works, that these beams were
composed of negatively charged particles, being deflected by magnetic
and electric fields. His experimental setup enabled to measure the charge-
to-mass ratio of negative particles, being the currently recommended
value [10]: |q |/m=1.75882001076(53) ×1011 C/kg. When Thomson ob-
tained such value, he noticed that the same quantity for Hydrogen ions
(measured through electrolysis in liquids) was around 2000 times smaller,
that is:
 # #
 |q | ## |q | ##
 ≈ 2000 . (1.3)
 m# beam m# H
As a consequence, there were two possibilities: either the module of the
electric charge of the beam elements would be two thousand times greater
than the module of the electric charge of the Hydrogen ions; or else the

6 1. Old quantum physics

FIGURE 1.2 Simplified scheme of a cathode ray tube with its elements to determine the
electron charge-to-mass ratio.

mass of the beam elements would be 2000 times less than the mass of
the Hydrogen ions. Thomson believed in the second hypothesis, consid-
ering that the electric charge module for the elements of the beam and
the Hydrogen ions would be the same. With these observations, he pro-
posed that the cathode rays are composed of corpuscles, which in turn are
fundamental elements of atoms. As a consequence, Thomson suggested
the divisibility of the atom and then, in 1904, the Plum Pudding. In this
model, negative charges (plums) are embedded in positive charges (pud-
ding), satisfying the discovered criteria. The name electron was given only
later, naturally, since the electrical phenomenon had been studied through-
out the 19th century, as, for example, in electrolysis. A simplified scheme
of a cathode ray tube used by Thomson is presented in Fig. 1.2, and the
detailed description in Box 1.2.

 ! The historical importance of this experiment lies in the proposal
 that atoms are divisible, composed of particles with charge equal
 in magnitude but opposite in sign. The negatively charged particle
 would have mass around two thousand times less than the posi-
 tively charged particles. These results led Thomson to propose the
 existence of the electron (originally named corpuscle) and to the de-
 velopment of an atomic model named Plum Pudding....

ter William Crookes’s and other scientists’ works, that these beams were
composed of negatively charged particles, being deflected by magnetic
and electric fields. His experimental setup enabled to measure the charge-
to-mass ratio of negative particles, being the currently recommended
value [10]: |q |/m=1.75882001076(53) ×1011 C/kg. When Thomson ob-
tained such value, he noticed that the same quantity for Hydrogen ions
(measured through electrolysis in liquids) was around 2000 times smaller,

As a consequence, there were two possibilities: either the module of the
electric charge of the beam elements would be two thousand times greater

1.1.4 Black body radiation
 A body, at a given temperature T, emits radiation. Why can’t we see the
radiation emitted by the objects around us? Because the radiation emitted
by all matters at room temperature is outside the visible spectrum range.
To see such radiation, we need to heat them. Who has never heated a piece
of metal until it turns red? Exactly! The object starts to emit radiation in
the visible range.
 Historically, the classic description of this phenomenon has failed for
large values of frequency f of the electromagnetic waves emitted. The
mathematical solution of this problem was proposed by Planck when
quantifying the energy of the system, definitely opening the door to the
world of quantum physics. In this section, we will describe the classical
model for thermal radiation and then the energy quantization solution.

 A black body absorbs all the radiation incident upon it and emits radi-
ation corresponding to its temperature T. A simple model for this system

16 1. Old quantum physics

 FIGURE 1.5 Simplified scheme of the experimental setup for observing the photoelectric
 effect.

 by Philipp Lenard, from 1888, with his experiments on cathode rays. In a
 few words, the experiment on the photoelectric effect was carried out by
 emitting monochromatic light on a metal plate (cathode) which, in turn,
 is inserted in a vacuum tube. This light-matter interaction promotes the
 emission of electrons, closing a small circuit. See Fig. 1.5.
 The experimental results provided the following observations:
(1) By applying a reverse potential difference, the electrons can be slowed
 down and the electric current in the circuit can be interrupted. From
 this, it is possible to measure the kinetic energy of electrons:

 T = eVc , (1.47)

 where e represents the electron charge and Vc the threshold potential,
 which depends on the material from which the cathode is made.
(2) The intensity of the incident light does not affect the kinetic energy of
 the ejected electrons, but only the quantity of electrons.
(3) The emission of electrons only occurs when the frequency of the inci-
 dent wave is above a certain value, which is known as threshold fre-
 quency (which depends on the metal). Below this threshold frequency,

1.1 Experimental basis 17

 no electrons are emitted, regardless of the value of the incident light
 intensity.
 In 1905, Einstein considered the light as particles (photons), with en-
ergy E = hf, in order to interpret these results, following the results of
Planck model for the black body radiation (see Subsection 1.1.4). This idea
explains the totality of the experimental observations: (i) an increase in
the intensity of the light beam corresponds to an increase in the num-
ber of photons and, consequently, in the number of ejected electrons from
the metal (cathode), but not in the kinetic energy; and (ii) the photon en-
ergy, according to Einstein’s hypothesis, would be totally transferred to
the electron which, in turn, would use this energy to leave the metal (work
function W ) and the remaining energy would be the kinetic energy. Con-
sequently, there is a threshold frequency, below which the photons are not
able to transmit enough energy to the electrons to overcome the work func-
tion of the metal, keeping the experimental circuit opened. In this case, no
matter how intense the incident light is, the electron cannot overcome the
work function of the material.
 Based on these ideas, Einstein formulated the following equation (en-
ergy conservation) for the photoelectric effect:

 hf = eVc + W ⇒ eVc = hf − W (1.48)

 ! The historical importance of these experiment and theory lies in
 the proposal to consider light as a particle. From these results, and
 based on the knowledge previously established by the scientific
 community in which light would be an EM wave, the concept of
 wave-particle duality for the light began to be discussed. The exper-
 imental setup developed by P. Lenard was also important because,
 later, in 1897, J. Thomson used cathode rays to study and propose
 the existence of the electron (see Section 1.1.3).

 ! Philipp Lenard (1862–1947): Born in Bratislava (now Slovakia, but
 then Hungary). He was awarded the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physics
 for his work with cathode rays, where we can highlight studies on
 the photoelectric effect from 1888 onward.
 Albert Einstein (1879–1955): Born in Ulm, Germany. The relation-
 ship of this illustrious physicist and scientist with the topic in ques-
 tion is the proposal to treat light as a particle, photons....

1.1.6 Charge of electron
 As of 1910, R. Millikan carried out a series of experiments to determine
the charge of the electron. The methodology was to spray oil into a cham-
ber, producing electrically charged droplets. The falling (without electric
field) and rising (with electric field) velocity of droplets were recorded. By
repeating the experiment for several droplets, he was able to determine
the elementary charge of the electron. Details about Millikan’s experimen-
tal apparatus can be found in Box 1.5.

 ! The historical importance of this experiment was to demonstrate
 the existence of an elementary electric charge, as well as to de-
 termine its value. These results supported the quantum theory in
 formation at the beginning of the 20th century.

 ! Robert Millikan (1868–1953): Born in Morrison, USA. As the main
 achievement of his scientific path, this experiment in which he de-
 termined and verified the elementary nature of the electron charge,
 stands out. Due to the success of his experiments, he was awarded
 the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics.

 As of 1910, R. Millikan carried out a series of experiments to determine
the charge of the electron. The methodology was to spray oil into a cham-
ber, producing electrically charged droplets. The falling (without electric
field) and rising (with electric field) velocity of droplets were recorded. By

Particle-wave duality
 Based on these findings, a simple question arises: since there is a wave-
particle duality for light, why not for matter? Reflecting on this idea, L.
Raymond, seventh Duke of Broglie, in 1924, based on the results of Ein-
stein’s Theory of Relativity from 1905, proposed that matter also has a
wavelength λ proportional to its momentum p , through the equation:

 h
 λ= (1.59)
 p

This idea, known as de Broglie hypothesis, will be better discussed in Sec-
tion 1.3, since the purpose of this section is only to present the experiments
that evidenced and consolidated the first ideas of quantum theory.
 Proceeding with the historical events, a few years later, in 1927,
C. Davisson and L. Germer realized that the angular dependence of elec-
tron diffraction by matter (Nickel) was the same as that observed for

22 1. Old quantum physics

x-rays, obeying, therefore, Bragg’s Law – discussed previously. Indepen-
dently, G. Thomson observed the same effect in metallic films. These
experiments confirmed de Broglie’s postulate and, consequently, the dual
behavior of matter.

 ! The historical importance of de Broglie hypothesis, together with
 the experimental confirmation by Davisson–Gremer and Thomson,
 is immense and we will return to this subject in Section 1.3. In a nut-
 shell, it was the opening of a new concept, where the matter could
 now be described as a wave. With these ideas, modern quantum
 theory was born.

 ! Louis Raymond (1892–1987): Born in Dieppe, France, he was the
 seventh Duke of Broglie. He proposed the wave nature of matter,
 which enabled the birth of modern quantum physics. For his con-
 tribution, he was awarded the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physics.
 Clinton Davisson (1881–1958): Born in Bloomington, USA. He was
 awarded the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physics for the experimental
 performance of electron diffraction in Nickel, thus confirming the
 Louis de Broglie hypothesis. The prize was shared with G. Thom-
 son.
 George Thomson (1892–1975): Born in Cambridge, England. He
 was awarded the 1937 Nobel Prize in Physics for the experimen-
 tal performance of electron diffraction in films, thus confirming the
 Louis de Broglie hypothesis. The prize was shared with C. Davis-
 son.
 William Bragg: Interestingly, Bragg’s Law was formulated by a fa-
 ther (William Henry Bragg [1862–1942]) and son (William Lawrence
 Bragg [1890–1971]), who shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics for
 their services in the analysis of crystal structure by means of X-rays.

 1.2 Bohr model for the atom

 In 1913, Niels Bohr, grounded in the experimental and theoretical re-
sults obtained by the scientific community so far (spectral lines of Hy-
drogen atom, charge-to-mass ratio for electron and black body radiation),
proposed an atomic model, based on the planetary model, as shown
in Fig. 1.8. Nonetheless, according to the classical laws of physics, as
known by Bohr, this model had a problem. Accelerated charges emit radi-
ation and, consequently, lose energy. Bohr’s planetary model for classical
physics could not be stable, and the electron would collapse in spiral,
emitting radiation continuously....

24 1. Old quantum physics

 1.2.1 Bohr’s postulates
 Bohr’s planetary model had problems, such as the atomic instability
 and, consequently, the continuous emission of radiation. For these reasons,
 Bohr presented some postulates:
(1) Orbits have discrete radii. With this postulate, Bohr solved the problem
 of the electron continually losing energy, performing a spiral move-
 ment, and collapsing close to the nucleus.
(2) Electrons are able to change orbits by absorbing/emitting radiation
 with frequency f and energy E = hf . See Fig. 1.8. This postulate is
 based on the black body and photoelectric effect experiments.
(3) Bohr postulated that orbital angular momentum must be quantized,
 varying in multiples of !: L = n!, where n = 1, 2, 3, · · · . This postulate is

 1.3 de Broglie hypothesis

 Up to the date of the de Broglie hypothesis (1924), the dual behavior for
light was well established, with the support of the double slit experiments
(1801), for example, and the experiments and theory for the photoelectric
effect (1905). Therefore, the hypothesis for a dual behavior for the matter
emerged as a sustainable proposal.
 In the Bohr model for the atom, the electron’s path is circular and well-
defined. However, de Broglie inaugurated a new phase of interpretations
of the orbits, considering them as waves (see Fig. 1.10). In order to be com-
mensurable and avoid destructive interference, there must be exactly an
integer number of wavelengths at the perimeter of the orbit. Therefore:

 2π r = nλ. (1.79)

Considering Eq. (1.59), the equation above may be rewritten as follows:
 h
 2π r = n ⇒ L = n!. (1.80)
 p

Therefore, with the de Broglie hypothesis, it is possible to recover, natu-
rally, one of Bohr’s postulates that requires the quantization of the angular
momentum.

1.4 Semi-classical quantization rule 29

 The transition from the classical physics to the modern quantum
physics, passing by the old quantum physics, would naturally be related to
the Lagrangian and/or Hamiltonian formalism, since the scientific com-
munity at the beginning of the 20th century was very comfortable with
the treatment and use of those tools. Therefore, it was natural to present
a quantization rule using the conjugate variables of the problem. W. Wil-
son (1915), J. Ishiwara (1915) and A. Sommerfeld (1916) independently
proposed the so-called semi-classical quantization rule (SCQR), given
by:
 .
 pi d q i = n i h (1.81)
 E
where pi are the generalized momenta; qi the generalized canonical co-
ordinates; ni a positive integer; and h the Planck constant. Note that
the integral above represents the area in the phase space {pi , qi }, for
a given energy value. From this proposal, it is immediately appar-
ent that each generalized coordinate has its associated quantum num-
ber.
 It is interesting to note that Sommerfeld–Wilson–Ishiwara SCQR (1915)
can be recovered from the de Broglie hypothesis (1924) – see Fig. 1.10. Ob-
serve: to avoid destructive interference, the perimeter of the orbit must
contain an integer number of wavelengths (similarly to what we did in
the previous section). Therefore:
 .

 λ

Taking Eq. (1.59) into the equation above, we recover the semi-classical
quantization condition (Eq. (1.81)). With this reasoning, we can see that
n ≥ 1, as in each orbit perimeter there must be at least one wavelength.
 To better understand the SCQR, let’s look at three examples: (i) a har-
monic oscillator, (ii) revisit the Bohr atom and (iii) the Sommerfeld model
for the atom.

 ! Arnold Sommerfeld (1868–1951): Born in Königsberg, today Kalin-
 ingrad (Russian exclave). He developed important models in old
 quantum physics, such as the semi-classical quantization rule and
 the atomic model that bears his name, considering elliptical orbits
 for atoms.
 William Wilson (1875–1965): Born in Goodyhills, United King-
 dom. Independently, he dedicated himself to generalizing the Bohr
 model, also considering elliptical orbits.
 Jun Ishiwara (1881–1947): Born in Tokyo, Japan. Independently, he
 dedicated himself to the study of semi-classical quantization rule.

1.4.3 Sommerfeld model for the atom
 Objective The Sommerfeld atomic model was motivated, mainly, by
 the experimental results of the splitting of spectral lines of Hydrogen
 when submitted to an electric field (Stark Effect – 1913) or magnetic
 field (Zeeman Effect – 1896). In an attempt to explain these phenom-
 ena, Sommerfeld proposed a model (1916) where the electron has an
 elliptical trajectory, therefore being a generalization of the Bohr model.
 See Appendix 1.A for a review of the geometric properties of the ellipse
 – concepts that will be useful throughout this subsection.

56 2. Construction of quantum theory I: wave mechanics

for describing systems of continuous variables, such as the position of the
electron in atoms.
 Objective The goal of this chapter is to deduce the Schrödinger equation
 and explore key ideas in wave mechanics, such as the wave function.
 We will also delivery essential concepts of quantum mechanics, such as
 probability density, operators, measurements, and important theorems
 such as Virial and Ehrenfest – all based on the postulates of quantum
 mechanics. Additionally, we will provide a thorough explanation of the
 wave packet and the corresponding Heisenberg uncertainty principle.

 2.1 Formulation of Schrödinger equation

2.1.1 Time-dependent equation
 Let’s consider a particle with mass m and total energy given by:

 E = T + V, (2.1)

where T = p 2 /2m represents the kinetic energy, p is the linear momentum,
and V the potential energy. We also consider ψ(x , t ) as the wave function,1
at position x , at a given time t . Since we are dealing with a wave, we can
write:
 ψ(x , t ) = Aei (k x −ωt ) , (2.2)
where k = 2π /λ is the wave vector. Considering the de Broglie hypothesis
λ = h/p , it is possible to conclude that:

throughout this book.

Eq. (2.2) can be written as follows:

 2.3 Example: infinite potential well

where the energy spectrum was obtained using the SCQR. In this section,
we will revisit the problem; however, using the Schrödinger equation. For
this purpose, let’s consider a particle of mass m confined in an infinite
potential described by Eq. (1.B.5) and represented in Fig. 1.14.

 parallel for comparison with other, more complex problems, such as
 the finite well, for example.

tential (x > a and x < 0). For this reason, we solve the time-independent
Schrödinger equation only for the region where V (x ) = 0. In this case, we

tute the fundamental mathematical basis for representing physical observ-
ables. These objects obey some basic properties, which we now describe.

 !

 In this subsection, we are just presenting the properties of the oper-
ators. However, we can say that the non-commutation of operators is a
fundamental characteristic of quantum mechanics – defying our classical
intuition. This means that, in quantum systems, the order in which opera-
tors are applied can affect the results of the measurements. The Heisenberg
uncertainty principle (discussed in more detail in Section 2.6) is a direct
consequence of this non-commutation. This concept establishes that the
precision in which we know certain pairs of conjugate variables, such as
position and linear momentum of the particle, is limited. The more precise
we try to measure one, the less precisely we can measure the other. This is
not due to technical limitations of measuring instruments, but it is intrinsic
to the quantum nature of particles.

which we are going to introduce some of the most important ones.

FIGURE 3.1 Stern–Gerlach experimental setup. The beam of Silver atoms leaves the oven
(1) and passes through a collimator (2), to then enter the region of magnetic field gradient
(3). Due to the quantization of the angular momentum, dots (4) on the screen should be
observed, while in the classical prediction, without quantization of angular momentum, only
a continuous line (5) would be observed. Adapted from reference [18]. Wikimedia Commons.
Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

 Objective The goal of this chapter is therefore to introduce the mathe-
 matical formulation related to matrix mechanics and, in order to em-
 phasize the equivalence of the physical concepts, we will make a close
 connection with the postulates of quantum mechanics. As a conceptual
 tool, we will use the Stern–Gerlach experiment.

 3.1 Stern–Gerlach experiment

 In Chapter 1, the Bohr model (1913) was described, which is based on
three postulates: (i) orbits with discrete radii, (ii) emission/absorption of
radiation hf due to the transition of electrons between these orbits, and
(iii) quantization of orbital angular momentum. Around the 1920s, this
model was still accepted and, for this reason, experiments were carried
out in an attempt to verify the quantization of physical quantities, such as
angular momentum.
 Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach carried out important experiments in
the years of 1921 and 1922. An oven was used to evaporate Silver atoms
(Ag), where the beam was collimated and passed through a region of in-
homogeneous magnetic field. At the end of the trajectory, the atoms were
deposited on a glass plate for later analysis. See Fig. 3.1. This entire appa-
ratus, however, is under vacuum. Why did Stern and Gerlach use Silver?
This atom has 46 electrons in a closed shell and 1 valence electron, there-
fore being a Hydrogen-like atom.
 To carry out this experiment, the magnetic field through which the
beam passes must be inhomogeneous; otherwise, only a torque is gen-
erated in the associated magnetic moment. Given this inhomogeneous
magnetic field, a deflection force emerges, which can be analyzed. We can

FIGURE 3.1 Stern–Gerlach experimental setup. The beam of Silver atoms leaves the oven
(1) and passes through a collimator (2), to then enter the region of magnetic field gradient
(3). Due to the quantization of the angular momentum, dots (4) on the screen should be
observed, while in the classical prediction, without quantization of angular momentum, only
a continuous line (5) would be observed. Adapted from reference [18]. Wikimedia Commons.

 Objective The goal of this chapter is therefore to introduce the mathe-
 matical formulation related to matrix mechanics and, in order to em-
 phasize the equivalence of the physical concepts, we will make a close
 connection with the postulates of quantum mechanics. As a conceptual
 tool, we will use the Stern–Gerlach experiment.

 3.1 Stern–Gerlach experiment

 In Chapter 1, the Bohr model (1913) was described, which is based on
three postulates: (i) orbits with discrete radii, (ii) emission/absorption of
radiation hf due to the transition of electrons between these orbits, and
(iii) quantization of orbital angular momentum. Around the 1920s, this
model was still accepted and, for this reason, experiments were carried
out in an attempt to verify the quantization of physical quantities, such as
angular momentum.
 Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach carried out important experiments in
the years of 1921 and 1922. An oven was used to evaporate Silver atoms
(Ag), where the beam was collimated and passed through a region of in-
homogeneous magnetic field. At the end of the trajectory, the atoms were
deposited on a glass plate for later analysis. See Fig. 3.1. This entire appa-
ratus, however, is under vacuum. Why did Stern and Gerlach use Silver?
This atom has 46 electrons in a closed shell and 1 valence electron, there-
fore being a Hydrogen-like atom.
 To carry out this experiment, the magnetic field through which the
beam passes must be inhomogeneous; otherwise, only a torque is gen-
erated in the associated magnetic moment. Given this inhomogeneous
magnetic field, a deflection force emerges, which can be analyzed. We can

3.1 Stern–Gerlach experiment 95

start by considering the magnetic field B" = (Bx , 0, Bz ), where Bx and Bz
depend only on x and z, respectively. Observe that the beam, when leav-
ing the oven, is aligned along the y axis. The forces acting on the Silver
atoms can then be written as:
 ∂
 Fx = (µx Bx + µz Bz )
 ∂x
 ∂ Bx ∂ Bz
 = µx + µz , (3.1)
 ∂x ∂x
 Fy = 0, (3.2)
 ∂
 Fz = (µx Bx + µz Bz )
 ∂z
 ∂ Bx ∂ Bz
 = µx + µz , (3.3)
 ∂z ∂z
where µx and µz are the components of the atomic magnetic moment
along x and z, respectively. Above, we considered that Bx = Bx (x ) and
Bz = Bz (z). Thus, ∂ Bx /∂ z = ∂ Bz /∂ x = 0. We can also consider that the
gradient along the x axis is small and, therefore, ∂ Bx /∂ x ≈ 0. After these
assumptions, Eqs. (3.1)–(3.3) can be rewritten as:

 ∂ Bz
 Fx ≈ 0, Fy = 0 and Fz = µz . (3.4)
 ∂z
 Therefore, there is a force acting on the Silver atoms. This force depends
on the field gradient and on the atomic magnetic moment. The classical
physics at that time described that the atomic magnetic moment could be
written as the product of the current I due to a charge q , multiplied by the
area A of the circular orbit with radius r of the particle around the nucleus.
Therefore, the classical atomic magnetic moment is given by:
 q
 µ = IA = v r, (3.5)
 2
where v is the speed of the particle as it precesses around the nucleus (in
the classical model)....

 We begin this section defining some relevant mathematical objects. The
vector |n$, called ket in Dirac notation, is the first of them, being equivalent
to a vector n" in Euclidean space. Considering a d -dimensional space, |n$ is
a column vector with d rows × 1 column:

On the other hand, &n| is also a vector, called bra in Dirac notation, this
being the conjugate transpose of a ket |n$, that is:

 &n| = |n$† . (3.8)

This property makes clear the usefulness of Dirac notation and how diffi-
cult it would be, for example, to represent, in a simple way, the conjugate
transpose with the Euclidean space notation. Bra is therefore represented
by a row vector, that is, 1 row × d columns:
 ' (
 &n| = n∗1 n∗2 · · · n∗d (3.9)

 Since we know bra’s and ket’s, we can now write &m|n$ as the inner
product, equivalent to m" ∗ · n" in the Euclidean space. Considering that all
vectors in space are orthonormal, there are only two possible results for
the inner product: one or zero. We then have:

 &m|n$ = δmn (3.10)

The normalization of space vectors is guaranteed through the equation:
 )
 1= &n|n$. (3.11)

 With these elements, the Hilbert space can be defined, which is:
1. a generalization of Euclidean space;
2. d -dimensional (finite or infinite), consisting of an inner product (Eq.
 (3.10)); and
3. described as an orthonormal set of vectors {|n$}, for example. Other vec-
 tors can be written in terms of this set of vectors, as follows:

Regarding item 3 above, we can understand that the vector |# $ can be rep-
resented as a superposition of orthonormal basis vectors {|n$}. Compare
Eq. (3.12) with Eq. (2.41). Therefore, in the Hilbert space, writing a vector
|# $ in terms of other vectors represents, from the physical point of view, a
superposition of eigenstates.
 We can compare the concepts presented in this section with those pre-
sented for the ‘Postulate for quantum states’ (page 65). In an analogous
way, we can revisit that postulate and state that a quantum state must be
completely represented by a vector |# (t )$ in the Hilbert space.

ators do not have explicit time dependence, except when there is a time
variation of the observable (example: time-dependent magnetic or electric
field). In the vector space, TDSE (see Eq. (2.10)), can be written as follows:

ized, we have:

3.B Simple correspondence between wave mechanics and matrix mechanics 113

Appendix 3.B Simple correspondence between wave mechanics
 and matrix mechanics

 In the initial chapters of this book we described the wave mechanics of
matter, where the wave functions ψn (x ) are solutions of the Schrödinger
equation, and also represent eigenstates in which the system can be found.
In this chapter, we introduced the matrix mechanics, which uses linear
algebra to describe the same quantum phenomena. In this case, the vectors
|n$ are the solutions of an eigenvalue equation, and they also represent
eigenstates in which the system can be found.2
 Concisely, we can write a wave function ψn (x ) as the projection of a
vector |n$ in basis |x $:

 ψn (x ) = &x |n$. (3.B.1)

These position vectors form an orthogonal basis and, since it is a continu-
ous space, the orthogonality condition can be written as:

 &x |x , $ = δ (x − x , ), (3.B.2)

while the completeness relation reads as:
 8
 d x |x $&x | = 1. (3.B.3)

From these results, we can verify the normalization condition of states in
both approaches:
 -8 .
 &n|n$ = &n| d x |x $&x | |n$
 8
 = d x &n|x $&x |n$ (3.B.4)

resulting in:
 8
 &n|n$ = d x ψn∗ (x )ψn (x ). (3.B.5)

 The equation above demonstrates a correspondence between the wave
functions ψn (x ) and the vectors |n$. It is important to emphasize that both
approaches (wave and matrix mechanics) describe the same quantum phe-
nomena.

2 In matrix mechanics, we often designate the eigenstate |n$ as just state.

118 4. One-dimensional problems: bound and unbound states

 4.A.3 Standard deviation, uncertainty principle 164
 Appendix 4.B Exercises 165

 In this chapter, we discuss bound states, such as harmonic oscillators
and potential wells, and unbound states, like tunneling through barri-
ers. This conceptual basis is very important in condensed matter physics,
for example. Bound states provide information about semiconductors and
quantum dots used in optoelectronics, while unbound states with tunnel-
ing are vital for understanding and developing various devices, such as
tunneling electron microscopes.
 ObjectiveThe goal of this chapter is therefore to solve simple one-
 dimensional problems, putting into direct practice the solution of the
 Schrödinger equation. The development and understanding of these
 models will provide a solid basis for more advanced studies in this
 book.

 4.1 Bound states I: harmonic oscillator

4.1.1 Description
 The quantum harmonic oscillator (QHO) model is used in several areas
of physics, such as to explain the specific heat of solids or the quantization
of the electromagnetic field. For this reason, this model is of great impor-
tance and deserves special attention, as well as a detailed description, with
different formalisms. Let’s therefore consider a particle with mass m sub-
mitted to a potential such as:

 1
 V (x ) = mω2 x 2 , (4.1)
 2
where ω is the angular frequency of the oscillator.
 Objective The goal of this section is to determine the energy spectrum,
 wave functions, and probability density of the particle confined in this
 potential.

4.1.2 Solution I: Hermite differential equation
Eigenstates
 We begin addressing this problem by considering the time-independent
Schrödinger equation, which can be expressed as:

 Appendix 4.B Exercises

Conceptual exercises
Exercise 4.1. Consider the idea of bound and unbound states, as discussed
along this chapter. Answer the following questions:
1. Discuss the meaning of bound and unbound states in the context of a
 one-dimensional potential well.
2. Explain the key difference in the energy spectra for these two cases.

Exercise 4.2. Consider the quantum harmonic oscillator (QHO) and an-
swer the following questions:
1. Why does the ground state energy of this system never reach zero?
2. Explain why the QHO has a finite probability density beyond the clas-
 sical turning points.
3. Compare the probability density distribution of the QHO with the clas-
 sical probability density, especially near the classical turning points.
4. Explain why the probability density of a classical harmonic oscillator is
 qualitatively different from that of a QHO for small values of n.
5. Describe the Correspondence Principle in the context of a harmonic os-
 cillator.

Exercise 4.3. Describe the concept of quantum tunneling.

Text-based exercises
Exercise 4.4. Verify that Eqs. (4.19)–(4.22) are solutions of the Hermite dif-
ferential equation, for the respective values of n.

166 4. One-dimensional problems: bound and unbound states

Exercise 4.5. Consider the potential for the delta well: V (x ) = −α δ (x ).
What is the dimension of the parameter α ?

Exercise 4.6. Rewrite Eq. (4.193) in terms of the energy of the infinite po-
tential well (Eq. (1.B.10)).

Exercise 4.7. Calculate the values of (kn a )2 from Fig. 4.8, where perfect
transmission occurs.

Practice exercises
Exercise 4.8. Consider a QHO in the ground state. Calculate the probabil-
ity of finding it beyond the classical turning points.

Exercise 4.9. Obtain the value of 5x̂ 6 6 for the quantum harmonic oscillator.

Exercise 4.10. Demonstrate that 5p̂ 6 = 0 for the harmonic oscillator using

electric charge −e and mass me ) form the fundamental elements of the Hy-
drogen atom, which will now be described in detail. Since mp ≈ 1836me ,
we assume that the center of mass of the system (and, consequently, the
origin of the coordinate system) coincides with the position of the proton.
Furthermore, the reduced mass5 of the system is approximately equal to
the mass of the electron. To simplify the notation, we take me = m, which
is an acceptable approximation. Within this framework, we consider the
electron to be under the influence of a Coulomb potential:

ergy of the Hydrogen atom is quantized, being inversely proportional to

does not depend on the other quantum numbers, such as the magnetic
quantum number m or the orbital quantum number l . These discrete en-
ergy levels are represented in Fig. 5.3, where an interesting effect can be
observed: for a given energy En , distinct confinement regions are estab-
lished by the effective potential Vef (r ), depending on the value of l . Thus,
it is reasonable to assume that the expectation value of the radius for a
given state depends on both n and l . This relationship will be analyzed in
detail later in this chapter.

 Application 5.A Periodic table

 In this section, we discuss the arrangement of the periodic table of the
elements based on the knowledge obtained for the Hydrogen atom up
to this point. We know that the periodic table has its elements grouped
and ordered according to their physical and chemical properties, such
as atomic mass, ionic radius, electronegativity, metallic character, etc. Ini-
tially, this arrangement was made in a phenomenological way. However,
nowadays, we know the physical and chemical foundations of this ar-
rangement – and the knowledge of the Hydrogen atom is an excellent
starting point.
 Objective The goal of this section is to understand the construction of
 the periodic table of the elements based on the studies of the Hydrogen
 atom, more precisely on the quantum number (n, l , m).

 We start this explanation with the first element of the periodic table,
the Hydrogen atom, with just one electron. Let’s assume that this electron
is in the ground state, that is (n = 1, l = 0, m = 0), which corresponds to
the 1s state. Multi-electron atoms are built from this Hydrogen atom in
the ground state, following the aufbau principle,10 where the addition of
an extra electron corresponds to the building of a new atom. However, in
which orbital will this new electron be added? In the most stable orbital,
following Madelung energy ordering rule, which says:
10 From German Aufbauprinzip, i.e. building-up principle.

204 5. Traditional problems with central potential

FIGURE 5.9 (a) Pauling diagram constructed in accordance with the Madelung energy
ordering rule. With this diagram it is possible to understand the arrangement of the periodic
table of elements. (b) Division of periodic table into blocks.

• States with lowest values of (n + l ) are filled first, and
• In cases of equal (n + l ) values, the state with the lower n value is filled
 first.
 From the Madelung energy ordering rule (MEOR) we can construct the
Pauling diagram, which is presented in Fig. 5.9(a). The first column, in
yellow, represents the orbital quantum number l = 0, that is the s subshell
– from n = 1 (K) shell to n = 7 (Q) shell. The small number in parenthe-
ses represents the sum n + l of the subshell. The next column, in blue, is
similar, however it represents l = 1, that is p subshell. The next column, in
pink, represents l = 2 (d subshell) and, finally, the last column corresponds
to l = 3 (f subshell). Following the MEOR (observe the small numbers in

 Application 5.A Periodic table

 In this section, we discuss the arrangement of the periodic table of the
elements based on the knowledge obtained for the Hydrogen atom up
to this point. We know that the periodic table has its elements grouped
and ordered according to their physical and chemical properties, such
as atomic mass, ionic radius, electronegativity, metallic character, etc. Ini-
tially, this arrangement was made in a phenomenological way. However,
nowadays, we know the physical and chemical foundations of this ar-
rangement – and the knowledge of the Hydrogen atom is an excellent
starting point.
 Objective The goal of this section is to understand the construction of
 the periodic table of the elements based on the studies of the Hydrogen
 atom, more precisely on the quantum number (n, l , m).

 We start this explanation with the first element of the periodic table,
the Hydrogen atom, with just one electron. Let’s assume that this electron
is in the ground state, that is (n = 1, l = 0, m = 0), which corresponds to
the 1s state. Multi-electron atoms are built from this Hydrogen atom in
the ground state, following the aufbau principle,10 where the addition of
an extra electron corresponds to the building of a new atom. However, in
which orbital will this new electron be added? In the most stable orbital,
following Madelung energy ordering rule, which says:
10 From German Aufbauprinzip, i.e. building-up principle.

204 5. Traditional problems with central potential

FIGURE 5.9 (a) Pauling diagram constructed in accordance with the Madelung energy
ordering rule. With this diagram it is possible to understand the arrangement of the periodic
table of elements. (b) Division of periodic table into blocks.

• States with lowest values of (n + l ) are filled first, and
• In cases of equal (n + l ) values, the state with the lower n value is filled
 first.
 From the Madelung energy ordering rule (MEOR) we can construct the
Pauling diagram, which is presented in Fig. 5.9(a). The first column, in
yellow, represents the orbital quantum number l = 0, that is the s subshell
– from n = 1 (K) shell to n = 7 (Q) shell. The small number in parenthe-
ses represents the sum n + l of the subshell. The next column, in blue, is
similar, however it represents l = 1, that is p subshell. The next column, in
pink, represents l = 2 (d subshell) and, finally, the last column corresponds
to l = 3 (f subshell). Following the MEOR (observe the small numbers in
parentheses in Fig. 5.9(a)): 1s is the only subshell with n + l = 1, being
therefore the most stable one and, consequently, the first to be filled. Then,
we find only one subshell with n + l = 2, that is 2s subshell, and it is filled
after 1s subshell. Continuing aufbauprinzip with MEOR, there are two sub-
shells with n + l = 3: 2p and 3s ....

 In this chapter, we study the angular momentum, a fundamental physi-
cal quantity that plays a crucial role in various phenomena and contributes
to the understanding of concepts such as magnetism.
 Objective The goal of this chapter is therefore to present the formal
 algebra of angular momentum (which can be orbital or spin) and its
 consequences. Understanding this chapter is fundamental to begin the
 studies in the next chapter, where we will study the addition of angular
 momenta.

220 6. Angular momentum

 6.1 Commutation relations

 We begin this chapter’s journey with the definition of angular momen-
tum:
 " = r" × p",
 L (6.1)
which, obviously, has components:

 " = Lx x̂ + Ly ŷ + Lz ẑ.
 L (6.2)

These components can be written in terms of the Levi-Civita symbol !ij k
(see Appendix 6.A for more details). Considering further that these quan-
tities are operators, we have:

 L̂i = !ij k x̂j p̂k , (6.3)

where the subscript index, in this case i , j , k , represents, respectively, the
Cartesian components x , y , z. Note also that x̂j is a generalization of the
spatial coordinate, and can be x̂ , ŷ , or ẑ, depending on the value assigned
to the associated index. We leave as an exercise the verification that the
components of a vector product can be represented as in the above equa-
tion.
 Our goal in this section is to determine the commutation relations for
the angular momentum – and the detailed proof to obtain this result is
given in Box 6.1. We therefore have:

 [L̂u , L̂v ] = i !!uv w L̂w (6.4)

which leads to:

 [L̂x , L̂y ] = i !L̂z , (6.5)
 [L̂z , L̂x ] = i !L̂y , (6.6)
 [L̂y , L̂z ] = i !L̂x . (6.7)

The result above indicates that the components of angular momentum do
not commute with one another. Consequently, it is physically impossible
to have simultaneous and precise knowledge of two of these quantities.
Mathematically, this means that the matrices representing these compo-
nents cannot be diagonalized simultaneously, as they cannot share the
same vector basis.

222 6. Angular momentum

 6.2 Angular momentum algebra

 Since the components of angular momentum do not commute with
each other, they cannot be determined simultaneously and with absolute
precision.1 For this reason, we can determine only one of these compo-
nents. To better understand the angular momentum, we therefore need
another operator, but one that commutes with these components. Thus,
we consider:
 L̂2 = L̂2x + L̂2y + L̂2z . (6.15)
Based on the definition above and the results from Section 6.1, it is possible
to determine the algebra of the angular momentum.

 Theorem 6.1 The operator L̂2 commutes with the components L̂u of an-
 gular momentum:
 [L̂2 , L̂u ] = 0 (6.16)

 Proof. Considering u = z:

 [L̂x L̂x + L̂y L̂y + L̂z L̂z , L̂z ] (6.17)
 = [L̂x L̂x , L̂z ] + [L̂y L̂y , L̂z ] + [L̂z L̂z , L̂z ]
 = L̂x [L̂x , L̂z ] + [L̂x , L̂z ]L̂x + L̂y [L̂y , L̂z ] + [L̂y , L̂z ]L̂y
 = L̂x (−i !L̂y ) + (−i !L̂y )L̂x + L̂y (i !L̂x ) + (i !L̂x )L̂y
 = 0.

 This same idea applies to other directions, and it is left as an exercise.
 "

 Therefore, L̂2 commutes with all components of the angular momen-
tum operator and thus we can simultaneously know the projection of the
angular momentum along a given axis, as well as its magnitude. We are
free to choose one of the components of angular momentum as a refer-
ence. By convention, we choose L̂z . What we will do from now on through
theorems, lemmas, and definitions are to obtain eigenvalues and vectors
corresponding to these two operators: L̂2 and L̂z .

1 This concept was discussed for the position-linear momentum [x̂ , p̂ ] = i !, with conse-
quences for problems studied throughout this book, such as plane wave and harmonic
oscillator.

6.2 Angular momentum algebra 223

 Definition 6.1 |a , b% are vectors of operators L̂2 and L̂z , being a and b,
 respectively, their eigenvalues:

 L̂2 |a , b% = a |a , b% and L̂z |a , b% = b|a , b%. (6.18)

 This definition is appropriate since L̂z and L̂2 commute. The goal of
 this subsection is to determine the values of a and b.

 Definition 6.2 L̂± = L̂x ± i L̂y are operators, known as raising and low-
 ering.

 Based on this definition, we can determine the other components of an-
gular momentum:

 1 1
 L̂x = (L̂+ + L̂− ) and L̂y = (L̂+ − L̂− ). (6.19)
 2 2i
Because these are observables, the angular momentum operators are Her-
mitian, while the raising and lowering operators are non-Hermitian.

 Theorem 6.2 The raising and lowering operators do not commute with
 each other:
 [L̂± , L̂∓ ] = ±2!L̂z (6.20)

 Proof.

 [L̂+ , L̂− ] = [L̂x + i L̂y , L̂x − i L̂y ] (6.21)
 ! "
 = [L̂x , L̂x ] − i [L̂x , L̂y ] + i [L̂y , L̂x ] − i [L̂y , L̂y ]

 = −i [L̂x , L̂y ] + i [L̂y , L̂x ]
 = −2i [L̂x , L̂y ]
 = 2!L̂z .

 The case [L̂− , L̂+ ] = −2!L̂z is left as an exercise for the reader. "

 Theorem 6.3 The component L̂z of angular momentum do not commute
 with the raising and lowering operators:

 [L̂z , L̂± ] = ±!L̂± (6.22)

224 6. Angular momentum

Proof.

 [L̂z , L̂+ ] = [L̂z , L̂x + i L̂y ] (6.23)
 = [L̂z , L̂x ] + i [L̂z , L̂y ]
 = i !L̂y + i (−i !)L̂x
 = !L̂+ .

The case [L̂z , L̂− ] = −!L̂− is left as an exercise for the reader. "

 Corollary 6.1 The operator L̂2 commutes with the raising and lowering
 operators:
 [L̂2 , L̂± ] = 0 (6.24)

 Proof. We know that the raising and lowering operators are linear with
 L̂x and L̂y . These, in turn, commute with L̂2 , according to Theorem 6.1.
 Thus, it is natural that [L̂2 , L̂± ] = 0. "

 to operators L̂2 and L̂z : L̂± L̂∓ = L̂2 − L̂2z ± !L̂z ....

simultaneous knowledge of two components of angular momentum is
impossible. We also deduced Eqs. (6.48) and (6.49), which tell us, respec-
tively,+that we can simultaneously know the angular momentum magni-
tude l (l + 1)! and its projection m! along the z axis. Note also that the
projection of angular momentum on the z axis is quantized, being an inte-
ger multiple or half-integer multiple of !. Despite these results, below we
will explore what we know about the components x and y of the angular
momentum.
 In order to obtain the expectation value of L̂x and L̂y , Eq. (6.19) is
required, which relates these operators with the raising and lowering op-

probable.

232 6. Angular momentum

FIGURE 6.1
 + Schematic representation of an angular momentum l = 3. We can measure
its module l (l + 1)! and its projection m!, but we cannot define its orthogonal components.
Therefore, the angular momentum has an equal probability of being found anywhere on the
surface of the cone. Furthermore, for the maximum projection value m = l , the vector does
not lie along the z axis.

Furthermore, for this case,+the projection of the vector on the z axis, i.e. l ! is
smaller than the module l (l + 1)! of the angular momentum. With these
arguments we can conclude that, for the case of maximum projection of the
angular momentum, it is not absolutely aligned along the z axis. Fig. 6.1,
despite being a classical representation of the angular momentum, assists
in its visualization.
 In Appendix 6.B we will discuss the Schrödinger uncertainty principle
(or generalized), applied to the angular momentum. This discussion will
complement the ideas presented above.

254 7. Addition of angular momenta

servables, which are essential for understanding how angular momenta
combine. The discussion then expands to the Hilbert space associated with
multiple angular momenta and the corresponding Clebsch–Gordan co-
efficients, applicable to up to N spins. Finally, the chapter connects the
theoretical framework to practical applications, such as the calculation
of magnetic moments (requiring the addition of orbital and spin angular
momenta), and the total angular momentum of atoms (analyzed through
Hund’s Rules).
 Objective The goal of this chapter is to extend the study of angular mo-
 mentum to systems involving multiple angular momenta. It aims to
 provide a comprehensive understanding of how angular momenta in-
 teract and sum up, forming their bases of commuting observables. The
 chapter introduces the mathematical tools necessary to describe these
 systems, including the expansion of the Hilbert space and the deriva-
 tion of change of basis matrices using Clebsch–Gordan coefficients.
 This chapter also explores applications, such as magnetic moments and
 the coupling of atomic angular momentum.

 7.1 Interactions between angular momenta

 In this section, we introduce Hamiltonians that describe interactions be-
tween angular momenta. The purpose of this presentation is to provide
physical insights that motivate the addition of angular momenta. For a
more in-depth discussion on the physical mechanisms underlying these
interactions, we refer the reader to reference [17].
Heisenberg: This isotropic interaction originates from the superposition
 of the atomic orbitals of two neighboring ions (which, for simplicity, we
 are considering a spin-only contribution). This Hamiltonian can be writ-
 ten as follows:

 Ĥ = −J Ŝ"1 · Ŝ"2 . (7.1)

 For J > 0 the spins are ordered parallel, while for J < 0 the spins are or-
 dered antiparallel. Note that J regulates the intensity of the interaction.
Ising: This is a particular case of the Heisenberg Hamiltonian and has an
 anisotropic character, where the spins are along the z axis. The mathe-
 matical formulation of the Hamiltonian is given by:

 Ĥ = −J Ŝ1z Ŝ2z . (7.2)

7.1 Interactions between angular momenta 255

XY: Similarly to the previous case, this interaction has an anisotropic
 character where the spins are on the xy plane, with the Hamiltonian
 formulation given by:

 Ĥ = −J (Ŝ1x Ŝ2x + Ŝ1y Ŝ2y ). (7.3)

Antisymmetric: This interaction points the angular momenta orthogo-
 nally to each other. For simplicity, we are considering only the spin
 contribution and thus this Hamiltonian can be written as:

 Ĥ = d" · (Ŝ"1 × Ŝ"2 ). (7.4)

 Note that the parameter that regulates the intensity of the interaction
 is the d" vector. This term is also known as the Dzialoshinsky–Moriya
 interaction.
Spin-orbit: The orbital angular momentum L̂ " of an electron can inter-

 act with its own spin angular momentum Ŝ". The parameter ζ gives the
 intensity of this interaction and will be further discussed in Applica-
 tion 7.B and Subsection 13.4.2. The corresponding Hamiltonian can be
 written as:
 Ĥ = ζ Ŝ" · L̂.
 " (7.5)

Local magnetocrystalline anisotropy: This Hamiltonian has an aniso-
 tropic character and originates from the spin-orbit interaction. In few
 words, this is the interaction of a spin with the crystal lattice....

256 7. Addition of angular momenta

 7.2 Commutation relations

 As we have seen above, there are several possibilities of interaction be-
tween angular momenta (and many others that were not mentioned) and
the addition of angular momentum depends on the system under consid-
eration.
 Objective Our goal for this section is to describe the set of commuting
 observables representing the physical system under study.

 To begin, let’s consider only two angular momenta: L̂" and L̂" , where
 1 2
each has its own Hilbert subspace, and these are independent. In this way,
we propose that the components of the angular momentum operators be-
longing to different subspaces commute with each other, such that:

 [L̂1u , L̂2v ] = 0, (7.8)

where (u, v ) = (x , y , z). The commutation relation above implies:

 [L̂21 , L̂2v ] = 0, [L̂22 , L̂1v ] = 0 and [L̂21 , L̂22 ] = 0. (7.9)

Furthermore, each subspace obeys the commutation rule of angular mo-
mentum (see Eq. (6.4)):

 [L̂1u , L̂1v ] = i !"uv w L̂1w and [L̂2u , L̂2v ] = i !"uv w L̂2w (7.10)

and, consequently, the entire algebra of angular momentum:

 L̂1z |l1 , m1 % = m1 !|l1 , m1 % and L̂21 |l1 , m1 % = l1 (l1 + 1)!2 |l1 , m1 %, (7.11)
 L̂2z |l2 , m2 % = m2 !|l2 , m2 % and L̂22 |l2 , m2 % = l2 (l2 + 1)!2 |l2 , m2 %. (7.12)

 Therefore:
 {L̂21 , L̂22 , L̂1z , L̂2z } (7.13)

forms a set of commuting observables represented by the vector |l1 , m1 % ⊗
|l2 , m2 % = |l1 , l2 , m1 , m2 %. This basis is known as local.
 However, for certain Hamiltonians, the local basis may not diagonalize
the operator, necessitating the use of an alternative basis. Let’s now focus
on the total angular momentum of the system, that is:

 " " "
 L̂ = L̂1 + L̂2 (7.14)

where
 " + L̂
 L̂2 = (L̂ " )2 = L̂2 + L̂2 + 2L̂
 " · L̂
 " , (7.15)
 1 2 1 2 1 2

7.2 Commutation relations 257

 L̂x = L̂1x + L̂2x , (7.16)
 L̂y = L̂1y + L̂2y , (7.17)
 L̂z = L̂1z + L̂2z , (7.18)
 L̂± = L̂1± + L̂2± . (7.19)

Since we aim to establish a new set of commuting observables that in-
corporates the total angular momentum, it is necessary to introduce addi-
tional commutation relations:

 [L̂2 , L̂21 ] = [L̂2 , L̂22 ] = 0. (7.20)

The details of these commutation relations are provided in Box 7.1. At
this stage, we have identified three commuting observables. However, the
local basis consists of four observables, meaning one additional observ-
able is needed. To address this, we examine another commutation relation,
which is demonstrated in detail in Box 7.2:

 [L̂2 , L̂z ] = 0. (7.21)

We therefore have a new set of commuting observables, with the same
number of quantum numbers as the local basis. The new set is:

 {L̂21 , L̂22 , L̂2 , L̂z } (7.22)

represented by vector |l1 , l2 , l , m%. This basis is known as coupled.
 How do the components of the total angular momentum commute with
one another? To begin, we can examine the commutation relation between
two components:

 [L̂x , L̂y ] = [L̂1x + L̂2x , L̂1y + L̂2y ] (7.23)
 = [L̂1x , L̂1y ] + [L̂2x , L̂2y ]
 = (i !)L̂1z + (i !)L̂2z
 = i !L̂z .

The other components are left to the reader verify. We can generalize the
above result as follows:

 [L̂u , L̂v ] = i !"uv w L̂w (7.24)

that is, the components of the total angular momentum follow the same
commutation relation as a single angular momentum. Consequently, the
total angular momentum follows the algebra discussed in the previous

chapter and therefore we know its eigenvalues and vectors (see Eqs. (6.48),
(6.49) and (6.50)):

 L̂z |l , m% = m!|l , m% and L̂2 |l , m% = l (l + 1)!2 |l , m% (7.25)...

 As we have seen above, there are several possibilities of interaction be-
tween angular momenta (and many others that were not mentioned) and
the addition of angular momentum depends on the system under consid-
eration.
 Objective Our goal for this section is to describe the set of commuting
 observables representing the physical system under study.

 To begin, let’s consider only two angular momenta: L̂" and L̂" , where
 1 2
each has its own Hilbert subspace, and these are independent. In this way,
we propose that the components of the angular momentum operators be-
longing to different subspaces commute with each other, such that:

7.3 Vectors in the coupled basis 261

 7.3 Vectors in the coupled basis

 In this section, we explain the process of constructing the vectors for a
system with N angular momenta. In Example 7.1, we demonstrated this
process for the simpler case of two angular momenta. To extend this to N
angular momenta, the approach involves iterative summation: first, com-
bine two angular momenta. Next, add a third angular momentum to the
result, then a fourth, and continue this process until all N angular mo-
menta have been incorporated. It is crucial to ensure that the total angular
momentum resulting from each step of the summation adheres to the con-
straint specified in Eq. (7.31).
 Objective The goal of this subsection is to establish a methodology
 to build the coupled basis vector, which can be sequential or non-
 sequential.

7.3.1 Sequentially coupled basis
 In this case, the angular momenta are added sequentially: first, the first
angular momentum is combined with the second. Next, the resulting total
is combined with the third angular momentum, followed by the fourth,
and so on, until the N -th angular momentum is included. The best way to
illustrate this process is through an example.
 ! Example 7.2

 Let’s consider four angular momenta: l1 = l2 = l3 = l4 = 1/2. As dis-
 cussed above, we should couple them as follows:

 " = L̂
 L̂ " + L̂
 " , (7.43)
 12 1 2
 " = L̂
 L̂ " + L̂" , (7.44)
 13 12 3
 " =L̂
 L̂ " = L̂" + L̂
 " . (7.45)
 14 13 4

 From Eq. (7.31), we have the following constraints:

 |l1 − l2 | ≤ l12 ≤ l1 + l2 , (7.46)
 |l12 − l3 | ≤ l13 ≤ l12 + l3 , (7.47)
 |l13 − l4 | ≤ l ≤ l13 + l4 , (7.48)

 which allow us to build the sequential coupled basis. First, we check
 the possible values for l12 , being: 1 and 0. Then, to build l13 , we add
 l3 and each possible values of l12 . For l12 = 1, we have two possible
 values of l13 : 3/2 and 1/2; and for l12 = 0, there is only one possible
 value of l13 : 1/2. To build l14 , we follow the same procedure. Fig. 7.1

262 7. Addition of angular momenta

FIGURE 7.1 Addition of four 1/2 angular momenta to build the sequential coupled basis.

 summarizes this idea. Now, to build the basis, we follow all the
 possible lines in that figure. Thus, the coupled basis is |l12 , l13 , l , m%,
 where m is the projection of the multiplet l on the quantization axis
 z. Note that this is a simplified notation, where the constant quan-
 tum numbers l1 , l2 , l3 , and l4 are omitted. Finally, the vectors are
 given by:

 |l12 , l13 , l , m% (7.49)
 |1, 3/2, 2, m%
 |1, 3/2, 1, m%
 |1, 1/2, 1, m%
 |1, 1/2, 0, m%
 |0, 1/2, 1, m%
 |0, 1/2, 0, m%

 Note that in the local basis we have four quantum numbers (m1 ,
 m2 , m3 , and m4 ), one for each angular momentum. Obviously, in
 the coupled basis, we have the same number of quantum num-
 bers. Furthermore, the two bases must preserve the dimension of
 /
 the Hilbert space. The local basis has dimension 4i =1 (2li + 1) =
 1)(2l2 + 1)(2l3 + 1)(2l4 + 1) = 16. The coupled basis has dimen-
 (2l1 +0
 sion l gl (2l + 1), where l represents each multiplet of the system,
 and gl its multiplicity. We then have for the coupled basis: one quin-
 tuplet (l = 2), three triplets (l = 1), and two singlets (l = 0), resulting
 in a Hilbert space with dimension (1 × 5) + (3 × 3) + (2 × 1) = 16. !

7.3 Vectors in the coupled basis 263

7.3.2 Non-sequentially coupled basis
 The angular momenta do not need to be added sequentially, as long
as they are always added in pairs – there is freedom of choice, which de-
pends on the system studied....

 We know that operators can be represented by matrices. Imagine that a
certain system has two angular momenta l1 = 1/2 and l2 = 1. We immedi-
ately know that the Hilbert subspaces have different dimensions: 2 × 2 and
3 × 3, respectively. How can we work with operators, which are matrices,
with different dimensions? The solution is to expand the Hilbert space to
 /
a total dimension N i =1 (2li + 1).
 Objective The goal of this subsection is therefore to describe the
 methodology for matrix expansion of system operators.

 To perform this task we can use the tensor products below:

 L̂1u = L̂u(1) ⊗ 1(2) ⊗ 1(3) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 1(N ) , (7.52)
 L̂2u = 1(1) ⊗ L̂u(2) ⊗ 1(3) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 1(N ) ,
 ..
 .

where u = (x , y , z). The subscript number outside the parentheses repre-
sents the n-th angular momentum, while the subscript number inside the
parentheses represents the Hilbert subspace of the m-th momentum. For
example, L2x represents the component x of the second angular momen-
tum, while 1(2) represents the identity operator in the subspace of the
second moment. If this subspace refers to an angular momentum l2 = 2,

 7.5 Local basis vs. coupled basis: Clebsch–Gordan coefficients

 In the previous section, we discussed how to expand the Hilbert space
for a system with N spins, i.e., how to obtain the operators under consider-
ation in the correct dimension. Now, how to change the operators from the
local basis to the coupled basis? To do this, we need to obtain the Clebsch–
Gordan matrix – a matrix that contains all the coefficients that relate the
vectors of the local basis to the vectors of the coupled basis. First, we will
discuss the coupling of 2 angular momenta, and then the coupling of 3
angular momenta to obtain a recurrence relation for N angular momenta.
However, the reader may be wondering: Why? One of the primary goals
when working with operators is to determine their eigenvalues, which re-
quires diagonalizing the operator. Depending on the operator under study,
a common approach to achieve this is by transforming the basis from local
to coupled.
 Objective The goal of this section is therefore to obtain the Clebsch–
 Gordan matrix – a matrix containing all the coefficients that relate the
 local basis vector to the coupled basis vector.

7.5.1 Coupling of 2 angular momenta
 Let’s consider the total angular momentum of the system:

pled basis |l1 , l2 , l , m%.

268 7. Addition of angular momenta

Raising and lowering operators
 If we consider m1 = m1max = l1 and m2 = m2max = l2 , consequently (as
discussed on page 258), m = mmax = l1 + l2 and l = lmax = l1 + l2 . For this
situation, there is only one possibility of states in the local and coupled
basis, being a univocal relationship:

 |l1 , l2 , lmax , mmax % = |l1 , l2 , m1max , m2max % (7.63)

When applying the lowering operator L̂− = L̂1− + L̂2− (Eq. (6.58)) 2lmax
times in the above equation, we can then find all vectors of lmax multi-
plet. To find the vectors of the lmax − 1 multiplet, we use the orthogonality
condition of the coupled basis vector:

 (lmax , mmax − 1|lmax − 1, mmax − 1% = 0 (7.64)

After that, it is possible to apply the lowering operators again. This pro-
cedure can be performed for all multiplets of the system, from l = lmax
to l = lmi n . The numbers associating one vector to another are known as
Clebsch–Gordan coefficients.

 was a mathematician renowned for his contributions to invariant
 theory, the development of Clebsch–Gordan coefficients, and the
 formulation of Gordan’s lemma.

 7.6 Basis change of an operator

 In the previous section, we determined the change of basis matrix, from
local to coupled (and vice versa). As we mentioned before, this matrix
allows us to (i) write the coupled basis vector in terms of the local basis
vector (and vice versa) (ii) change the basis of an operator. Why change
the basis? In many cases, the operator is not diagonal in the local basis
but becomes diagonal in the coupled basis. Diagonalizing the operator is
essential because it allows us to access its eigenvalues, which are critical
for understanding its properties.

278 7. Addition of angular momenta

 Objective The goal of this section is to use the change of basis matrix
 and exemplify the methodology of how to take a given operator from
 the local basis to the coupled basis.

 To change the basis of the operator, we highly recommend revisiting
Appendix 3.A, where Eq. (3.A.6), presented below, is derived:

basis matrix, Û † is the conjugate transpose of the change of basis matrix,
and finally Aa is the operator before the change of basis. As has been done
throughout this book, let’s look at an example, which will make the ideas
clearer.

 ! Pieter Zeeman (1865–1943): Born in Zonnemaire, in the province
 of Zeeland, Netherlands. He was awarded the 1902 Nobel Prize in
 Physics for his research on the influence of magnetism on radiation
 phenomena.
 Alfred Landé (1888–1976): Born in Elberfeld, Germany. He had
 Arnold Sommerfeld as his PhD advisor, with the Landé factor, dis-
 cussed above, being one of his main contributions.

 Application 7.B Angular momentum of atoms and the Hund’s
 rules

 Atoms have several electrons, and, in this case, how can we add their
angular momenta or, at least, have some idea? Complete atomic shells do
not contribute to the total angular momentum because their net contribu-
tion is precisely zero. Therefore, only the electrons in the incomplete shells
contribute to the total angular momentum of the atom. In the case of light
atoms (with an atomic number less than 75), the spin angular momentum
of each electron couples to produce an effective spin:
 %"
 Ŝ" = Ŝi , (7.B.1)
 i

that is, the effective spin angular momentum is the sum of the spin angular
momentum of each electron. Similarly, the orbital angular momenta also
couple, resulting in an effective orbital angular momentum:
 " = % L̂
 L̂ " . (7.B.2)
 i
 i

These angular momenta, Ŝ" and L̂,
 " interact through spin-orbit coupling to
produce the total effective angular momentum:

 Ĥ = ζ Ŝ" · L̂
 " (7.B.3)

7.B Angular momentum of atoms and the Hund’s rules 283

where ζ is the spin-orbit parameter. For heavy atoms (atomic number
greater than 75), each electron couples its spin and orbital momentum to
produce its own total angular momentum. These individual total angular
momenta then couple to produce an effective total angular momentum:

 " %"
 Jˆ = Jˆi . (7.B.4)
 i

This last case is known as j − j coupling.
 Based on the discussion above, we are able to introduce the Hund’s
rules:
Hund’s first rule: effective spin momentum According to the Pauli ex-
 clusion principle, no more than two electrons can occupy the same or-
 bital (the two electrons must have opposing spins). To minimize electron
 repulsion, the orbitals are filled one by one and then, after all are filled,
 the first orbital receives a second electron (with opposite spin, ‘down’
 in this case). This means that the effective spin must be at its maximum
 value. This is Hund’s first rule.
Hund’s second rule: effective orbital momentum For a given effective
 spin, there are several possible values for the effective orbital momen-
 tum, but the main question is: which configuration minimizes the energy
 of the system? The answer also lies in the electronic repulsion: if all
 the electrons precess in the same direction,4 this minimizes the chance
 of these electrons meeting each other. Therefore, for the energy to be
 minimum, the effective orbital momentum must be maximum....
